question: During Ziehl-Neelsen staining, which property of the mycobacterial cell wall allows the organism to resist decolourisation with acid-alcohol?

answers.text: High mycolic acid (waxy lipid) content in the cell wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mycobacteria possess a cell wall rich in mycolic acids — long-chain waxy lipids that form a hydrophobic barrier. Once heated carbolfuchsin penetrates this layer, the mycolic acid prevents acid-alcohol from washing the dye out, making the organism 'acid-fast'.

answers.text: Thick peptidoglycan layer similar to Gram-positive bacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mycobacteria do have peptidoglycan, it is their unique mycolic acid content (not peptidoglycan thickness) that confers acid-fastness. Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan but are NOT acid-fast — they are easily decolourised by acid-alcohol.

answers.text: Outer lipopolysaccharide membrane similar to Gram-negative bacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mycobacteria do not possess an LPS-containing outer membrane. Their cell wall is uniquely rich in mycolic acids covalently linked to arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan. LPS is a feature of Gram-negative bacteria and does not confer acid-fastness.

A polysaccharide capsule (as in Cryptococcus or Streptococcus pneumoniae) protects against phagocytosis but has no role in staining properties. Acid-fastness is due to the waxy mycolic acid in the mycobacterial cell wall.

overallFeedback.feedback: Acid-fastness is due to mycolic acid — a unique waxy lipid in the mycobacterial cell wall. Do not confuse this with peptidoglycan (Gram-positive retention) or LPS (Gram-negative outer membrane). The mycolic acid barrier is the reason ZN staining requires heating the carbolfuchsin.

Mycolic acid is the key to acid-fastness. These long-chain waxy lipids (C60–C90) form a hydrophobic barrier that resists aqueous decolourisation. This is why heat is needed to drive carbolfuchsin in — and why, once in, it cannot be washed out by acid-alcohol.
